The program is meant to print a substring of argv[0], but it may end up printing some portion of memory located above argv[0]. This issue is similar to a buffer overflow resulting from the use of a "safe" string function (such as strncpy()) where the size argument is allowed to get out of sync with the size of the buffer.

Windows provides the _mbs family of functions to perform various operations on multibyte strings. When the following members of the _mbs family are passed a malformed multibyte string, such as a string containing a valid lead byte followed by a single null byte, they can read past the end of the string buffer and return a pointer to an invalid memory address: 
_mbsinc
_mbsdec
_mbsninc

The crypt() function is used for hashing and/or encrypting a password. The function takes two arguments: a key, which is the password, and a salt. Depending on the implementation and the value of the salt, crypt() may be using MD5, DES, Blowfish, SHA-256, or SHA-512 algorithms underneath. Both MD5 and DES are no longer recommended for use in security-sensitive contexts. Furthermore, if crypt() uses DES for its implementation, the salt is required to consist of only two characters, which is not long enough to sufficiently protect against brute-force attacks. If you are adding or modifying password file entries, the security of your application will also suffer if you pass the same value to crypt() for both the password to encrypt and the salt. By definition, the salt must be stored in the clear with the password, thus revealing the first two characters of the password and leaving only remaining characters for the attacker to guess.

Note: Fortify Static Code Analyzer will also report a Command Injection finding in the case where user-controlled data can modify the environment of a process execution. The finding is reported under the assumption that the process being run could modify its behavior because of the tainted environment it is running on. This is particularly true if the process is being run through a ShellShock vulnerable version of Bash shell in which case, an attacker will be able to run arbitrary commands by injecting a malicious environment variable.
Descriptions.Recommendations: Functions that cannot be used safely should never be used. If any of these functions occur in new or legacy code, they must be removed and replaced with safe alternatives. Assuming that the variable buf is a locally declared character array, replace all calls to gets(buf) with fgets(buf, sizeof(buf), stdin) or the C++ >> operator from a stream to a standard C++ string, such as: cin >> str. Be cautious! Using the same operator to read into a C-style char* string carries the same risk of buffer overflow as gets(). When using C11 or a more recent standard of the C language, consider using the Annex K gets_s(buf, read_size) function instead of gets(buf). The gets_s(buf, read_size) was added in C11 to provide a security-focused replacement for gets(buf).

Functions that cannot be used safely should never be used. If any of these functions occur in new or legacy code, they must be removed and replaced with safe alternatives. Replace all uses of >> buf, where buf is a C-style char* string with input to standard C++ strings defined in string.h, like this: >> str. Also consider using the SafeStr library from http://www.zork.org/safestr.

Functions that cannot be used safely should never be used. If any of these functions occur in new or legacy code, they must be removed and replaced with safe alternatives. Replace all calls to strcpy() and similar functions with their bounded counterparts, such as strncpy(). On Windows platforms, consider using functions defined in strsafe.h, such as StringCbCopy(), which takes a buffer size in bytes, or StringCchCopy(), which takes a buffer size in characters. On BSD Unix systems you can safely use strlcpy() because it behaves the same as strncpy() except that it always null-terminates its destination buffer. On other systems, always replace instances of strcpy(d, s) with strncpy(d, s, SIZE_D) to check bounds properly and prevent strncpy() from overflowing the destination buffer. For example, if d is a stack-allocated buffer, then SIZE_D can be calculated using sizeof(d). When using C11 or a more recent standard of the C language, consider using the Annex K strcpy_s() function instead of strcpy(). The strcpy_s() was added in C11 to provide a security-focused replacement for strcpy().

Use memchr() rather than rawmemchr(). memchr() takes the size of the buffer to be searched and returns null if the search character is not found within the buffer's bounds. If the buffer you are searching is a null-terminated string, then another option is to make use of the strchr() or strrchr() functions, which properly stop searching when a null-termination character is encountered. On some systems strchr() will be translated to __rawmemchr() by the compiler, which may cause Fortify Static Code Analyzer to report issues on code that seems to follow best practices. Use an explicitly-bounded call to memchr() to remedy this problem when it occurs.

Make sure that the size argument passed to memchr() always matches the size of the buffer to be searched. Do not rely on untrusted data to determine the buffer size. If the buffer you are searching is a null-terminated string, then another option is to make use of the strchr() or strrchr() functions, which properly stop searching when a NULL termination character is encountered.

Make sure that the size argument passed to memmem() always matches the size of the buffer to be searched. Do not rely on untrusted data to determine the buffer size. If the buffer you are searching is a null-terminated string, then another option is to make use of the strchr() or strrchr() functions, which properly stop searching when a NULL termination character is encountered.

Use caution when operating on multibyte strings with the _mbs family of functions. Avoid exposing these functions to malformed strings. Microsoft recommends using the isleadbyte(), _ismbslead(), ismbstrail() and _mbbtype() functions to test the validity of leading and trailing bytes and identify invalid multibyte strings [1].

If you are adding or modifying password file entries, make sure the crypt() function does not use MD5 or DES algorithms for its implementation. Select a random value for the salt to crypt(). Because the salt becomes public when it is encoded in the ciphertext, it is important to not use a value that is related to the password.

As a convention, replace all calls to strcpy() and similar functions with their bounded counterparts, such as strncpy(). On Windows(R) platforms, consider using functions defined in strsafe.h, such as StringCbCopy(), which takes a buffer size in bytes, or StringCchCopy(), which takes a buffer size in characters. On BSD Unix systems strlcpy() can be used safely because it behaves the same as strncpy() except that it always null-terminates its destination buffer. On other systems, always replace instances of strcpy(d, s) with strncpy(d, s, SIZE_D) to check bounds properly and prevent strncpy() from overflowing the destination buffer. For example, if d is a stack-allocated buffer, then SIZE_D can be calculated using sizeof(d). If your security policy forbids the use of strcpy(), you can enforce the policy by writing a custom rule to unconditionally flag this function during a source analysis of an application. See the Fortify Static Code Analyzer Custom Rules Guide for more information. Another mechanism for enforcing a security policy that disallows the use of strcpy() within a given code base is to include a macro that will cause any use of strcpy to generate a compile error: 
#define strcpy unsafe_strcpy

As a convention, replace all calls to sprintf() and similar functions with their bounded counterparts, such as snprintf(). On Windows(R) platforms, consider using functions defined in strsafe.h, such as StringCbPrintf(), which takes a buffer size in bytes, or StringCchPrintf(), which takes a buffer size in characters. On other systems, including BSD and other Unix and Linux platforms, always replace instances of sprintf(d, f, ...) with snprintf(d, SIZE_D, f, ...) to check bounds properly and prevent snprintf() from overflowing the destination buffer. For example, if d is a stack-allocated buffer, then SIZE_D can be calculated using sizeof(d). If your security policy forbids the use of sprintf(), you can enforce the policy by writing a custom rule to unconditionally flag this function during a source analysis of an application. See the Fortify Static Code Analyzer Custom Rules Guide for more information. Another mechanism for enforcing a security policy that disallows the use of sprintf() within a given code base is to include a macro that will cause any use of sprintf to generate a compile error: 
#define sprintf unsafe_sprintf

If the program is written for Windows(R), replace all calls to strlen() with the strsafe.h equivalents StringCbLength(), which takes a maximum buffer size in bytes, or StringCchLength(), which takes a maximum buffer size in characters. If the length of the provided string is greater than the specified buffer size, these functions return an error; otherwise they behave in the same way as strlen(). If the program is written for a platform where these bounded replacements are not available, consider implementing a proprietary bounded equivalent to strlen() that behaves in the same way as the strsafe.h functions StringCbLength() or StringCchLength(). If strlen() must be used, perform careful manual null-termination of strings before they are passed to strlen() and audit occurrences of strlen() to ensure the correct usage. You can use a custom rule to unconditionally flag this function for audit. See the Fortify Static Code Analyzer Custom Rules Guide for more information.

Tips.Tip: Be vigilant when auditing any program that uses the crypt() function: - Make sure MD5 and/or DES algorithms are not used for its implementation. - Verify that the same value is not used for both the salt and password, because the behavior of the underlying algorithm exposes characters from the password and makes it easier for an attacker to decrypt the encoded value. - The salt value should be a random value. If the same value or a predictable value is always used as the salt, an attacker may pre-compute a set of hashed passwords using the salt value and compare the set against the value encoded by the application.
